messages.body_plain:
Greetings!
I was a participant in the 2017 intermediate distance sampling course. I am trying to finish the analysis I was working on during the course and have run into a few data structural issues. My data are based on ship based line-transect surveys of Heaviside's dolphins off Namibia. I am trying to implement a mark recapture design using a pair of visual observers (tracker; platform 2) and a towed hydrophone array for acoustically detecting the dolphins (primary observer; platform 1). I have followed the methods in Burt et al. 2014 as best as possible regarding setting up my data table for a trial observer configuration and using a full independence model due to responsive movement issues of the dolphins being attracted to the boat.

I have around a dozen detections that do not have an associated perp distance but do contain group size and sea state information. I have coded these distances with a dummy variable as '-1'. From what I can tell, in R these detections are ignored when calculating the overall detection function and the detection function on the trackline. I am left with 37 duplicate detections and a handful missed by either the visual or acoustics platform. For estimating the detection functions, I included detections from 3 types of survey effort: dedicated transect legs, opportunistic transect legs, and transmitting legs. I understand that I can only use detections from dedicated transect legs to estimate density and abundance.

This is all going swimmingly until this point: I followed the golftee and crabsealMRDS.csv file examples from our distance sampling course. I notice that for both of these files, there are only rows of data that contain transect lines where animals/golftees were observed. The golftee dataset only has one transect line but to draw attention to the crabseal data, there should be some lines where no seals were observed. My data are arranged in a flat file format, nearly identical to the crabsealMRDS.csv. I have labeled my columns in the same manner. However, if I try to run a full independence trial observer configuration GLM in R using a csv file that contains any rows that do not have an object ID and relevant distance information, R immediately codes these blanks as 'NA' and gives me an error stating that 'no NAs can be included in the model'. The model crashes and thus, I don't know how to go about including any relevant dedicated transect legs which did not have animals observed to be used to calculate N. Further, I need to find a way to apply the estimated overall detection function and the detection function for the intercept to calculate N for the mark recapture data that were only included on dedicated legs. Lastly, here comes a monkey wrench-- I have additional visual and acoustic detections (as well as effort lines where no animals were detected) from dedicated transect legs on the surveys when only one observer platform was working -e.g., acoustic detections that occurred at night when the visual team was off effort OR visual detections that occurred when the hydrophone array was not deployed behind the boat. If I have understood the Burt et al. 2014 paper correctly, running a FI model with a trial observer configuration only provides the detection functions for the primary observer (acoustics platform). I would greatly appreciate if someone could please explain how I may go about including these single platform detections in R, and which detection function I should apply to the remaining visual detections when there was no acoustic combined effort. (I am assuming I can apply the detection function calculated by the trial observer configuration to the remaining acoustic detections when there was no combined visual effort as the acoustics platform is coded as primary observer.)

During the distance sampling course I was using the Distance software and did not use R outside of the software. At the very end of the class, Len realized that I will need to do this analysis in R instead of Distance. I am still not certain why this is the case. I have tweaked the provided code from the golftee and crabsealMRDS datasets in order to get this far in R. I am happy to send my data in flat file format and the code I'm currently stuck on if anyone thinks they can be of assistance!

Thank you,
Morgan Martin

Morgan

There was a lot packed into your email.  I don't pretend to have the answers to all of your questions; perhaps others will fill in some of the gaps.

I'll weigh in on the subject of transects without detections causing the MRDS analysis to fail with errors.

Working with the crabbieMRDS data set, I examined the data to learn there were 118 transects in that survey.  I isolated one transect (99A55) that had but a single detection.  I then, crudely eliminated that detection with the commands

crabr[crabr$Sample.Label=="99A55", "distance"] <- NA
crabr[crabr$Sample.Label=="99A55" & crabr$observer==1, "detected"] <- 0
crabr[crabr$Sample.Label=="99A55" & crabr$observer==1, "object"] <- NA
crabr[crabr$Sample.Label=="99A55" & crabr$observer==2, "object"] <- NA

I confirm that the function `ddf` in the MRDS package is not happy about that.

I don't know the details of the ungulate dataset analysed in Burt et al. (2014), but there may not have been empty transects in that dataset either.  There were 816 duplicates in that dataset.

I don't know the lower limit of the number of detections suitable for an MRDS analysis.  You note you have 37 duplicates--likely a companion symptom of having transects without detections.  I note in passing that the crabeater seal dataset upon which you are basing your setup has 1125 duplicate detections.

As you can understand, a distance sampling analysis fitting a detection function plus estimating g(0) is likely more data-hungry than an analysis where g(0) is assumed equal to 1.  I don't know if an MRDS analysis has been performed with datasets the size of yours.  Hopefully others can shed some light on this.

Hi Eric,

Thank you for your reply and shedding some light on the transect NA issue. The Burt et al. 2014 paper provides a very similar analysis to mine in their Example 2. PDF attached -- the use data from a pilot whale line-transect ship survey which had 50 duplicates, 63 detections by the tracker observer platform and 74 detections by the primary observer. My sample sizes would be similar if I had distance info for those dozen duplicates...bummer. Pages 9-10 in Burt et al. 2014 describe how they came to choose the full independence model with a trial observer configuration based on responsive movement, which is the same issue with my data.

I wonder if the MR model in Distance and R is only set up to handle data that are arranged with duplicate rows for each detection along the transect lines. This would make sense for following a step-wise method for first estimating the detection function overall and on the trackline before moving on to estimating density and abundance for those detections only on dedicated survey legs. If true, then my issues are partly resolved and the next step is to try to figure out how to apply the detection functions properly to the visual and acoustic detections on dedicated legs- when effort for both platforms is combined and when only one platform is on effort.

Simple summary of my data fitted to a full independence model with a trial configuration with distance and no covariates:
Summary for trial.fi <http://trial.fi> object
Number of observations               :  40
Number seen by primary               :  37
Number seen by secondary (trials)    :  37
Number seen by both (detected trials):  34
AIC                                  :  603.7714

Conditional detection function parameters:
              estimate        se
(Intercept) 2.09690643 0.7479803
distance    0.01337536 0.0172499

                            Estimate         SE              CV
Average p             0.7365978   0.01875208   0.02545769   #this is the overall detection function / empirical conditional detection funct.
Average primary p(0)  0.8906021   0.02230634   0.02504635 #this is the trackline detection function
N in covered region  50.2309389   1.68321612   0.03350955

.
Page 9 in the Burt et al. paper states. "The number of trials generated by the tracker and the number of duplicates are shown in Figure 5b, from which the empirical conditional detection function was obtained (0.772; Fig. 6). We fitted the MR model selected by Canadas, Desportes & Borchers (2004), which included perpendicular distance, Beaufort sea state and group size as explanatory variables (Fig. 6). From this model, the probability of detection on the trackline by the primary observer, given detection by the tracker, was estimated to be 0.796 (CV = 0.11)."  ---Does this mean it is possible to apply the 'empirical' overall detection function to both the visual and acoustic detections on dedicated transit legs? The acoustics platform is the primary observer in my study and I know that I should be able to use the above estimates of p and p(0) for the acoustic detections on dedicated legs as well as for any of the duplicates that were on dedicated legs. I have very few detections on dedicated legs from when only the visual platform was on effort. I am curious if I can apply these values of the detection functions to both platforms in this regard. If so, I can combine all dedicated transit leg effort lines into one flat file and treat any acoustic and visual detections as if they were from the same platform (and including all duplicates as only 1 detection per duplicate). Then I could estimate density and abundance for the area....feel free to call me crazy.

Thank you for any and all help!
Morgan

Sorry to hear you're having some trouble getting your data into mrds!

Some tips:

  - mrds doesn't use the flatfile format that the Distance R package
uses, so you'll need to format it in a particular way.
  - if you just want to fit a detection function (ignoring getting
abundance for now), you need to make a data.frame with the columns as
outlined in the "Details" section of the ddf manual page (see ?ddf). One
row per observation (observing the same animal twice == 2 rows)
  - once you have a detection function fitted to your satisfaction, you
can form the observation, sample and region tables, as described in
?dht. You can then use dht to get abundance estimates for those data
that you used to fit the detection function.
  - R has the special NA type to deal with missing data, it's generally
a bad idea to use codes such as -1 or -9999 to deal with missing data as
different packages can interpret them in different ways, NA is always
"not available".
  - detections that don't have perpendicular distances can be used for
abundance estimation, provided you think they have the same
characteristics as the data that you used to fit the detection function.
We don't currently have general software to deal with this, so you'll
need to do some manual calculation to include them.

There are a few things here but I'll try to be as concise as possible...

  - Regarding missing values: for Distance for Windows, -1 is fine. In R
NA is preferred (this is just a general point, not particular to mrds
analyses). More on this below.

  - when using ddf, you need to remove any missing values, that includes
those which are placeholders for transects that had no observations, as
well as those observations that don't have recorded distances. The dht
manual pages shows you how to format the sample, observation and region
tables to include the effort. So, based on the code you posted:

CH <- read.csv("CH Combined Visual and Acoustics Platforms on SE
Distance Trial.csv", header=TRUE)
CH <- subset(CH, distance!=-1)

fi.mr.dist <- ddf(method="trial.fi <http://trial.fi>",
                  mrmodel=~glm(link="logit", formula=~distance),
                  data=CH, meta.data=list(width=350))
summary(fi.mr.dist)

should be the right model I think. But as you say, the mode checking
doesn't look good.

  - regarding sample size and model form: although this is the model
that accurately reflects the way the data were collected, you're really
pushing mrds to its limits here, especially given the model checking
results. With more data one might want to include covariates to improve
the fit, but that doesn't seem to be an option here.

- mixing visual and acoustic data: ah okay, I see. Perhaps truncation
isn't such a big issue here, thanks for clarifying!

Hope this helps.

cheers,

Dear Dave,

Thank you very much for the help and advice. I have spent the day trying to find a way to use the detection function estimates calculated in R from ddf to apply to my single platform data for using dht to calculate abundance of the study area. I have searched through other posts on this forum and found a similar post but I am still not certain how to implement this is R. Regarding your comment:

 - when using ddf, you need to remove any missing values, that includes
those which are placeholders for transects that had no observations, as
well as those observations that don't have recorded distances. The dht
manual pages shows you how to format the sample, observation and region
tables to include the effort.

I have tried several ways of trying to subset the double platform MR data as a means to be able to include it in a single csv file with my single platform data to be able to subsequently run dht on the single platform data using the ddf model results from the MR data in R. The MR data used to calculate the detection functions contains mostly detections from non-dedicated transect legs. I have tried to include the dedicated transect single platform data as a second csv file and created data frames for region.table, sample.table and obs.table from these data but I have not been successful in using them to run dht with the MR model. I understand that this can be done in the Distance software in what seems to be a pretty easy manner:
Define a new data filter that selects the new subset of data. Note that it must be a subset of the data used to fit the detection function. Define a new Model Definition, and in the Estimate tab, check the option to Estimate density / abundance and
also the option to Use the fitted detection function from previous MRDS analysis. Select the ID of the analysis you want to use.

I think my issue is not knowing how to merge these two data sets in a way that allows me to do this in R. If I create a merged spreadsheet and include a column called 'duplicate' and include 1's for all rows containing MR data and then copy over all the single platform data (including empty transects) for when the ship was on dedicated transect legs -- I think I also would need to include a single row for each duplicate detection that was used in the MR analysis if it was on a dedicated leg. Then I could subset the data into an MR data set and a single platform data set by using the duplicate column. Do you have any ideas or advice for how to properly go about this? I've spent about 8 hours on this today and banging my head against my laptop at this stage.

This was the similar post answered by Eric from Feb. 26th:

Hi all,

I have a good sized single platform line-transect data set and for a small portion of it I was able to collect double platform data using trackers and a trial configuration. I have calculated g(0) and average p (Pa) from the trial data but I would like to generate density estimates from the full single platform dataset using mcds and correct using the g(0) or Pa in order to use all my data. I am using the mrds packing in R and there doesn't seem to be an option to implement Pa or g(0) when calculating density (using dht function).

Should I manually re-calculate density by replacing p with Pa in the equation D= n/N in covered area*p? Or Tiago's post on Friday made me think that perhaps I should apply something similar to what he suggested, see below.  There are a few papers that correct densities using the g(0) and I'm sure I'm missing a better way to do this. Any direction would be much appreciated.

>From a pragmatic point of view, in Distance you could simply fit a detection function to the data from island B, and then get the probability of detection (P) and the corresponding standard error (se) from the Distance analysis. Then you run an analysis of the data of Island A only, force Distance to use a Uniform detection function with no adjustments, and then add a multiplier that is the P with the corresponding se. In this way, distance will do all the correct calculations for you and the reported results will be the same as if you had used the data from B to get the detection probability and the data from A for the encounter rate, which I believe is what you want (Is the maximum detection distance in both islands about the same?).

Many thanks,

Gemma

Reply to Gemma:

With the scenario you describe, you'll need to live with the assumption that the g(0) you estimated for a portion of your dataset applies to the entire dataset.  To adjust your density estimate derived from the single platform survey, accounting for the g(0)<1, you would do this:

using the estimate of g(0) as what the literature calls a "multiplier".

The harder part of the adjustment is to incorporate the uncertainty in your estimate of g(0) into your adjusted estimate.  If we generically refer to an estimate of a multiplier as "c", then this formula for variance in density comes into play:

where the first term is the encounter rate coefficient of variation, the second term is coefficient of variation for the detection function and the third term is the coefficient of variation for your estimate of g(0).

Multipliers and their use in adjusting estimates, along with properly propagating uncertainty, is described in more detail in Buckland et al. (2001) Section 6.2.3

It is also the case that multipliers have been programmed into the graphical interface version of Distance.  Consult Chapter 8, Conventional distance sampling analysis--section entitled "Multipliers in CDS analysis" for further details.

 From Eric

I feel like there has to be a simple way to do this in R without needing to set up a new analysis from the beginning using the Distance software. If you or anyone can offer some advice it will be greatly appreciated! The single platform data and all dedicated transect effort lines from the combined double observer platform data including those which did not contain observations are attached in the spreadsheet with attempted tweak at R code. This spreadsheet would be all the data used to calculate N if it was able to be incorporated into the dht function.

Thank you,

Morgan

Dear distance samplers

I concluded my analysis some ago, yet looking at some of the results now, I get slightly confused.

Especially regarding how to present my findings.

1.      Why does df for many of my results have two decimals? - do you just remove the decimals, rounding the number?

df are determined both by the number of lines/points in your design and by the number of detections.  A Satterthwaite approximation is used to calculate them, and it does not give an integer value.  Probably simpler to round for quoting results.

2.      The CV seems to be calculated form the SE. Is that statistically allowed? - when CV is usually calculated from SD

CV can be defined either way.  The one that makes sense in the distance sampling context is se/estimate.

3.      Do you write your results as density +- SE and abundance +- SE? - or is it better to use the 95%CI in parenthesis after the results?

I would quote confidence limits – they’re more informative.  Whichever you use, make sure that it is clear to the reader what you are presenting.

4. Do reviewers prefer to have encounter rate and such included in the results section, or are density and abundance results usually enough? - the article is not a methods article.

It really depends on the purpose of your analyses – and on what a referee feels is required!  Generally, it’s better to give more rather than less, unless it confuses the message.  It’s easier to remove detail later than to add detail.  Or you can put the details of the analysis into an appendix.

Hi Morgan, hi listfolk,

I'm now getting a little lost on what you're trying to do here... sorry.

Am I right in thinking your aim now is to:

1. estimate g(0) from double observer data (with acoustic/visual platforms)
2. estimate detectability from a separate set of distance sampling data
3. estimate abundance by combining the p from 2. and the g(0) from 1.

?

If that's correct, you can't do this in one step in the mrds/Distance
packages in R. Abundance estimation (step 3.) needs to be handled
manually in R.

I'm a little unclear on exactly how to allocate effort here, certainly
the effort for 2. needs to be accounted for correctly, but one could
consider the g(0) estimate as an ad hoc correction to the abundance
estimation, in which case you can ignore effort for those observations,
and use the Distance R package to do 2 and 3, then post-hoc correct the
estimate by the g(0)? That would just mean dividing the abundance
estimate by the g(0) estimate. (You can do a bit better than this and
get a better variance estimate by including the info about the g(0)
uncertainty you get from fitting that model in mrds -- you can get there
by assuming independence and adding the squared CVs from the N and g(0).)

Hope that's helpful and answers the question. If not, feel free to reply
to me off-list and we can go back and forth to get an answer and then
post a full explanation for folks here.

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
James

Good  question, particularly for those coming from the Distance for Windows software.  When using the R package Distance with clusters, the answer is that size-bias regression is not performed, regardless of whether there are covariates in the detection function.

Distance in R uses a Horwitz-Thompson-like estimator to estimate abundance.  The "Expected cluster size" reported by Distance in R is actually the ratio of the estimated individual abundance divided by the estimated abundance of groups.  You could have a look at the documentation for the function `dht` in the package `mrds` in R help for a bit more detail.

The estimates you provided give a good example of size bias.  The average size of groups detected in a survey is usually an over-estimate of the size of groups in the population.  This is because small groups at large distances are less likely to be detected and therefore appearing in your sample.

The computed expected group size in your model without size in the detection function is 6.6; however when group size is included in the detection function, there is acknowledgement of the influence of group size on detectability.  The computed expected group size is smaller in the model that includes size as a covariate; consequently removing (some/all) of the over-estimation of group size in the population that is present when the effect of group size on detectability is not considered.

Hope that helps you.

messages.body_plain:
Use of R package Distance for analysis of distance sampling data

In the six months since the online material was made available, >2000 users have conducted >6000 sessions with the website

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/

We have continued to add learning material to the website.  Those wishing to know how to analyse distance sampling data using R, rather than Distance for Windows; this new material is for you.

There are no new principles of distance sampling associated with this material, because all that is described in this material is analysis using different software. As such there is only a single (short) lecture introducing you to differences between analysis using these two pieces of software. Much of that difference revolves around data organisation; because Distance for Windows takes care of data organisation matters; but with R, you must take more responsibility for organising distance sampling data.

Three exercises that were present in previous materials have been re-done using R.
duck nest data from Monte Vista refuge (Chapter 1)
Montrave point transect songbird data (Chapter 3) and
Hawaiian amakihi data (Chapter 5)

There is also an additional exercise that cannot be conduct using Distance for Windows. The analysis of this Scottish crossbill lure survey data is described in the lecture on multipliers in Chapter 6. These exercises are cross-referenced in the chapters where the theory is introduced.

Each of the exercises has a description and solution. Both the description and solution has a narrative highlighting important aspects of the material. We have also provided Rmarkdown files used to create the exercise narration. Those Rmarkdown files are supplemental and are not central to understanding analysis of distance sampling data using R.

We would appreciate hearing your comments about the addition of these materials.  We would be grateful if you would share this news with others who are interested in distance sampling but who are not subscribers to this Google group mailing list.
